ta-l1d13q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 13, which compares the Spirit's eternal procession with the Son's generation. Lombard asks first whether the proceeding Spirit can be called begotten like the Son, and why the Son is called both begotten and proceeding while the Spirit is only proceeding. He then asks how generation and procession differ, granting what we can know (the Spirit proceeds and is not begotten; the Son proceeds and is begotten) and confessing that we cannot fully explain how, since both are ineffable. Finally he asks whether the Spirit, not being begotten, should be called unbegotten, and denies it, reinterpreting a contrary text of Jerome. Four articles are announced: whether there is procession in God, whether one or several, how the two processions should be named, and whether the Spirit should be called unbegotten.
claims: The Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten; the Son both proceeds and is begotten.
The difference between generation and procession cannot be fully explained in this life.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3535.summary: First objection against procession in God. Procession implies a progressive motion, and every motion belongs to need and imperfection.
claims: Procession implies motion, which implies imperfection.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3538.summary: Second objection. Procession is the going out of one from another, which involves distance between them, and in the divine persons there is no distance at all.
claims: Going out implies distance.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3541.summary: Third objection. Every procession is from something into something, but the divine persons, being self-subsistent, are not from something into something.
claims: Procession is always from something into something.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3545.summary: Sed contra from John 15:26: the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.
claims: Scripture says the Spirit proceeds from the Father.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3551.summary: Second sed contra. The soul bears the image of the Trinity, and in it knowledge proceeds from the mind and love from both, so there is procession in the divine persons.
claims: In the image, knowledge and love proceed.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3554.summary: Thomas's determination. 'Procession' is said in two ways. It means local motion, properly the progressive motion of animals, which is in God only metaphorically, as when divine wisdom or goodness is said to proceed into creatures by producing its likeness in degrees. Or it means the bringing forth of what is originated from its principle, and since in God one person is from another as from a principle, there is procession in God properly in this sense.
claims: There is procession in God properly, as the origination of one person from another as principle.
Procession as local motion applies to God only metaphorically.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3557.summary: Reply to the first objection. In creatures every procession involves some motion or change, either local or in the source or the product. In God one person originates from another without change, as was said of generation, since nothing imperfect is predicated of God.
claims: Divine origination involves no change.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3560.summary: Reply to the second objection. Although there is no distance in place or essence between the divine persons, there is distinction of persons by personal properties, and that suffices for procession.
claims: Distinction by personal properties suffices for procession.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3563.summary: Reply to the third objection. Local procession is into something as its terminus, but what proceeds from a cause need not proceed into another, and that is how procession is taken in God.
claims: Procession from a cause need not be into another.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3575.summary: First argument that there is only one procession in God. As paternity marks the property of origin 'from whom someone is', so procession marks 'who is from another'. There is only one paternity in God (Dist. 7), so only one procession.
claims: There is only one paternity in God.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3578.summary: Second argument. In things of one nature in species, there is only one mode of communicating that nature; mice generated from putrefaction and from seed are not the same species (the Commentator). The divine nature communicated by procession is one in number as well as species, so there is only one mode of procession.
claims: One nature is communicated in only one mode.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3581.summary: Third argument. Operations are distinguished by their termini and principles. Divine procession always has the same principle, the producer's nature, and the same terminus, the divine nature received, so there is only one procession.
claims: Operations are distinguished by principles and termini.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3585.summary: Fourth argument. Two processions would differ either on the side of the essence or of the relations, since there is nothing else in God. On the side of the essence there is only conceptual diversity among attributes, which cannot cause the real plurality needed for two processions of really distinct persons. Nor on the side of the relations, since relations follow the processions in our understanding: the Son is Son because he proceeds from the Father.
claims: Neither essence nor relations can ground a real distinction of processions.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3588.summary: Sed contra. One procession has only one proceeding person, and in God there are two proceeding persons, Son and Spirit, so there must be two processions.
claims: One procession yields one proceeding person.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3591.summary: Thomas's determination. Some say the two processions are really distinct and there is no need to ask how, since they are the first things distinguishing the persons, as one does not ask how rational and irrational differ. This is unfitting: generation and procession have no opposition, and every formal distinction is by some opposition. Also, they are signified as operations, and things operating or operated are not distinguished by their operations; rather actions differ in species by the forms of their agents and motions by their termini. Others say the difference is that generation is a procession of nature and the Spirit's a procession of will. But will and nature are only conceptually distinct in God, and a merely conceptual distinction cannot ground a real one, since the principle is not weaker than what it grounds; and then the procession of intellect, by which the Son is Word, would differ from that of nature, by which he is Son. So in God there is no real distinction except by relations of origin, and the plurality of processions must be traced to them. There is a procession by which one person proceeds from one, generation, by which the Son is from the Father, said to be by way of nature or intellect, since he proceeds as Son and as Word, and in both modes one proceeds from one. There is another procession from two at once, from the one who proceeds and from the one from whom he proceeds. It is distinguished from the first by origin, since it is from the one proceeding by the first procession. It is called procession by way of will because one love can proceed from two willing in consent. By these modes of origin several persons are produced, distinct by relation of origin: the Son from the Father and the Spirit from both. So unless the Spirit were from the Son, no real distinction between Son and Spirit could be given.
claims: The processions cannot be distinguished as primitive realities, since they are not opposed, nor by nature and will, which are only conceptually distinct.
There are two processions: one from one (generation) and one from two, including the one proceeding (spiration).
Without the filioque there would be no real distinction between Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3594.summary: Reply to the first argument. Paternity signifies a determinate mode of origin that cannot be further multiplied by a different account of origin, only by matter, numerically. Procession signifies origin in general and can be determined in two modes: procession of one from one who does not proceed, and procession also from one who proceeds. No further modes can be distinguished by the account of origin, so there cannot be more than two processions. Distinguishing a procession from one proceeding person or from several would differ only as one and many, which has nothing to do with origin, as if 'walking' were divided by white and black rather than by two-footed and four-footed.
claims: Procession in general admits two determinations: from one non-proceeding person and from a proceeding person.
There can be no more than two processions in God.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3597.summary: Reply to the second argument. In created nature there are two communications, by way of nature and by way of love, and nature is communicated only in the first. It is from the imperfection of created will that nature cannot be communicated through it, since what proceeds by will, love, is not a self-subsistent hypostasis as in God. So it is from the perfection of the divine nature that it is communicated not only by the act of nature, generation, but by the act of will, the consent of love.
claims: Only in God is nature communicated also by way of will, because divine love is subsistent.
concepts: communication by nature and by love

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3600.summary: Reply to the third argument. The divine processions are distinguished by both principle and terminus. The divine nature is the principle of generation in the Father not absolutely as nature but as paternity, and the Son does not have his being Son from the nature as acquired by generation but from the nature's being, in reality, filiation in him. So the relations themselves stand in some way as principle and terminus of the processions.
claims: The relations function as principle and terminus of the processions.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3604.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Since the persons, who are really several, are distinguished by the processions, the processions cannot differ only conceptually; nothing causes a formally greater distinction than the one by which it is itself distinguished. As the personal properties are really identical with the essence but really several as relative, so the processions, compared to the nature as principle or terminus, differ only conceptually, as will and nature do. Compared to the relative properties as principle or terminus, they differ really.
claims: The processions differ really through their relation to the relative properties and only conceptually as compared to the nature.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3607.summary: Answers the remaining objection that relations follow the processions, so that the processions would cause the diversity of relations rather than the reverse, or there would be a circle. A divine relation is not only a relation but personal, constituting a person, and so it acts as the constitutive difference and proper form of the person whose operation is generation or spiration. So as relations they follow the processions and receive difference from them, while as proper forms of the persons they cause the difference of the processions, without a vicious circle.
claims: Relations follow the processions as relations but cause their difference as constitutive forms of the persons.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3619.summary: First argument that the Spirit's procession should be called generation rather than procession. If it is not generation, it is divided against generation, but nothing common is divided against what is proper, and procession is common to both.
claims: The common is not divided against the proper.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3622.summary: Second argument. Like the Son's generation, the Spirit's procession expresses a special mode of origin, or it would not constitute a person. 'Procession' expresses no special mode of origin.
claims: A constitutive mode of origin needs a special name.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3625.summary: Third argument. The Spirit receives the Father's whole nature and substance as the Son does, and the procession by which one receives the nature of one's source is called generation, even in lower things.
claims: Procession that communicates nature is generation.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3629.summary: Fourth argument from Damascene's definition of generation as a work of the divine nature in which the begetter undergoes no change and God is neither prior nor posterior. The Spirit's procession is a work of the divine nature, not of will, as Hilary shows: will gave substance to creatures, but nature gave it to the Son, and the Spirit is not a creature.
claims: The Spirit's procession is a work of the divine nature, fitting Damascene's definition of generation.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3635.summary: Sed contra. Whatever proceeds by way of generation proceeds as begotten, especially among living things. The Spirit does not proceed as begotten, otherwise there would be two sons in the Trinity.
claims: Whatever proceeds by generation is begotten.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3638.summary: Thomas's determination. In God one can distinguish common and proper, though not universal and particular, which would require a real diversity between communicable quiddity and proper being (Dist. 8), impossible in God. Common and proper are found in two ways: in reality, as the essence is common to the three and each person is distinguished by what is proper, and conceptually, when our intellect grasps something under both a common, indeterminate concept and a determinate, proper one. Both the concept of genus and of difference pertain to dignity, as with cognition (common) and science (proper) in God, though neither is the genus of the other as they are in God. Likewise 'procession' is said according to the common concept of origin and 'generation' according to a determinate concept. They relate as common and proper, not as genus and species.
claims: In God there is common and proper, really and conceptually, but not universal and particular.
'Procession' names origin in general and 'generation' a determinate mode, related as common and proper, not genus and species.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3641.summary: Reply to the first argument. Procession taken in its common concept is not divided against generation, but taken as the determinate mode of procession proper to the Spirit it is.
claims: As the Spirit's proper mode, 'procession' is divided against generation.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3644.summary: Reply to the second argument. Often a proper thing is named by a common name, as 'proprium' is retained for a convertible predicate not signifying what a thing is, because it adds no nobility for which it could be named. That is not the case here, since the Spirit's origin adds nothing to the concept and lacks nothing compared with the Son's generation, the Spirit being equal in dignity. Three reasons are given for the name. First, the Spirit most approaches procession, proceeding not only as the Son does but from one who proceeds. Second, procession is said in two ways, as local motion and as an effect's going out from its cause, and both fit the Spirit: as a distinct person, his procession resembles going out from a cause; as love, which tends toward another as object rather than as recipient, it resembles local procession from something into something, as the Father loves the Son with the love that is the Spirit. The Son's procession fits only the first. Third, which Thomas thinks better, in creatures we find something self-subsistent proceeding by way of nature, which we call generation, so we could name the Son's procession properly. We find nothing self-subsistent proceeding by way of love, so we could name the Spirit's procession only by a common name.
claims: The Spirit's procession is named by the common term chiefly because creatures offer no subsistent procession by way of love from which to name it.
'Procession' also suits the Spirit as proceeding from a proceeding person and as love tending into another.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3647.summary: Reply to the third argument. Procession of love as such does not communicate a nature; it does so in God, where nothing can be imperfect. So by the common account of his procession the Spirit is not one to whom a nature is communicated, and his procession cannot be called generation by its proper account, since communication of nature belongs to the very concept of generation. Conceptual diversity is not enough for a real difference of processions, but it is enough for different names.
claims: Communication of nature belongs to the concept of generation but not to the concept of love's procession.
Conceptual diversity suffices for different names though not for real difference.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3651.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Nature is the principle of the Spirit's procession not under the aspect of nature but under the aspect of will, from which love proceeds, so his procession is not called 'nativity', which is named from nature. It does not follow that the Spirit is a creature. Will relates either as principle to what it produces, and so to creatures, or to the very ground of producing, and so to love, the Holy Spirit, as intellect relates to art (Dist. 10).
claims: The Spirit's procession is from the nature as will, so it is not called nativity.
The will is related to creatures as products and to the Spirit as the ground of producing.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3664.summary: First argument that the Spirit should be called unbegotten, from Jerome's authority in Lombard's text.
claims: Jerome calls the Spirit unbegotten.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3667.summary: Second argument. An infinite (indefinite) term converts with negation given the subject's existence: whatever exists and is not a man is a non-man. 'Unbegotten' is such a term, so since the Spirit exists and is not begotten, he is unbegotten.
claims: Infinite terms convert with negation when the subject exists.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3670.summary: Third argument. 'Unbegotten' signifies either a relation or something absolute. It is not a notional relation, since then the essence could not be called unbegotten, so it is absolute and fits the Spirit.
claims: 'Unbegotten' is said of the essence, so it is absolute.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3674.summary: Sed contra from Lombard's text: only the Father is unbegotten.
claims: Only the Father is unbegotten.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3677.summary: Thomas's determination. In God nothing can properly be said privatively, since privation requires an aptitude to have what is lacking, which cannot befit God. So 'unbegotten' must be taken negatively, not privatively. Some negations negate within a determinate genus, which resembles privation in positing a genus; others are outside any genus, absolute negation. Taken as negation outside a genus, 'unbegotten' fits whatever exists and is not from another by generation, created or uncreated: the Father, the Spirit, the divine essence, and the first creatures, which did not come into being by generation. Taken as negation within a genus, it can be within the genus of the divine nature, fitting Father, Spirit, and essence, or within the genus of principle in the divine nature, fitting only the Father, and then it is the Father's notion. A principle can be known either by something's being from it, as the Father is known by active generation and spiration, or by its not being from another, as the Father's notion 'unbegotten'.
claims: In God nothing is said privatively; 'unbegotten' is a negation.
As negation outside a genus or within the divine nature, 'unbegotten' fits Father, Spirit, and essence; as negation within the genus of principle, it fits only the Father and is his notion.
concepts: negation in a genus vs. extra genus

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3680.summary: Reply to the first argument. Jerome takes 'unbegotten' to mean 'not begotten', as negation outside a genus or within the genus of the divine nature, not within the genus of principle.
claims: Jerome's usage is a non-notional negation.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3683.summary: Reply to the second argument. The negation of an infinite term is not a negation within a determinate genus but only within the genus of being, so it can be said of every being to which the affirmation does not apply. A negation within a determinate genus cannot be said outside that genus.
claims: Infinite terms negate within being as such; determinate negations only within their genus.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3686.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Unbegotten' as fitting only the Father signifies his notion and does not fit the essence. As fitting the essence and the Spirit, it signifies no notion and nothing absolute, since then it would fit the Son too; it removes a notion, passive generation.
claims: As said of the essence and the Spirit, 'unbegotten' removes passive generation rather than positing anything.

ta-l1d13q1-d1e3695.summary: An expositio textus. (1) Far be it to suspect anything like a mother between Father and Son, since then the Spirit's procession would seem material, the father being the active principle of generation and the mother the material one. (2) Augustine's 'I do not know, I am not able, I do not suffice' distinguish lack of acquired art, of natural power or industry, and of practice. (3) In the division 'everything is unbegotten, begotten, or made', the members vary by material, not formal, multiplication, so one member is repeated because it fits two, the Father and the Spirit.
claims: The Spirit is not a 'mother' in the Trinity, since that would make his procession material.
'Unbegotten' in the division is repeated because it fits both Father and Spirit.

ta-l1d13q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 13 maps Lombard's comparison of the Spirit's procession with the Son's generation: whether the Spirit is begotten, why the Son also proceeds, how generation and procession differ, and whether the Spirit is unbegotten. It announces four articles.

ta-l1d13q1-Dd1e3527.summary: Article 1 asks whether there is procession in God. Thomas distinguishes procession as local motion, metaphorical in God and used of wisdom's procession into creatures, from procession as the bringing forth of what originates from its principle, which is proper in God. Divine origination involves no change, distance, or terminus in another; distinction of persons by properties suffices.
claims: There is procession in God properly, as origination from a principle without change.

ta-l1d13q1-Dd1e3567.summary: Article 2 asks whether there is one procession or several. Thomas rejects grounding the distinction of processions in their being primitive, since they are not opposed, or in nature and will, which are only conceptually distinct. He grounds it in origin: one procession from one (generation, by way of nature and intellect, Son and Word) and one from two, including the one who proceeds (spiration, by way of will). Hence without the filioque Son and Spirit could not be distinguished. Procession in general admits only these two determinations. The processions differ really as related to the relative properties, which act as their principles and termini, and only conceptually as related to the nature. Relations follow the processions as relations but cause their difference as constitutive forms of the persons.
claims: There are exactly two processions, distinguished by origin: from one, and from two including the one proceeding.
The processions differ really through the relative properties and only conceptually through the nature.

ta-l1d13q1-Dd1e3611.summary: Article 3 asks why the Spirit's procession is called 'procession' rather than 'generation'. In God there is common and proper, really and conceptually, but not universal and particular. 'Procession' names origin in common and 'generation' a determinate mode, as common and proper, not genus and species. The Spirit's procession bears the common name chiefly because creatures offer nothing subsistent proceeding by way of love from which to name it. It is also apt because the Spirit proceeds from a proceeding person and, as love, tends into another. It is not generation because communication of nature belongs to the concept of generation but not of love, and because the nature is its principle as will, not as nature.
claims: 'Procession' and 'generation' relate as common and proper; the Spirit's procession has only a common name.
The Spirit's procession is not generation because it is from the nature as will.

ta-l1d13q1-Dd1e3656.summary: Article 4 asks whether the Spirit should be called unbegotten. Nothing is said privatively of God, so 'unbegotten' is a negation. As negation outside a genus or within the divine nature, it fits Father, Spirit, essence, and even the first creatures. As negation within the genus of principle, it fits only the Father and is his notion. Jerome uses the broader sense, and said of the Spirit it merely removes passive generation.
claims: The Spirit is unbegotten only in a non-notional sense; as a notion, 'unbegotten' belongs to the Father alone.

ta-l1d13q1-Dd1e3690.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 13 excludes any maternal, material principle in the Trinity. It glosses Augustine's confession of ignorance and explains the repeated member in the division of beings into unbegotten, begotten, and made.
claims: There is no material principle in the divine processions.

ta-l1d13q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 13 compares the Spirit's procession with the Son's generation. Article 1 holds that there is procession in God properly, as origination from a principle without change. Article 2 holds that there are exactly two processions, distinguished not as primitive realities nor by nature and will but by origin: one from one (generation) and one from two including the one proceeding (spiration). This again implies the filioque, and the processions differ really through the relative properties that act as their principles and termini. Article 3 explains that 'procession' and 'generation' relate as common and proper, and that the Spirit's procession bears the common name because creatures offer no subsistent procession of love from which to name it. Article 4 holds that 'unbegotten', a negation, fits the Spirit only in a broad sense, while as a notion it belongs to the Father alone.
claims: There are exactly two processions in God, distinguished by relations of origin.
The Spirit's procession is called by the common name 'procession' because creatures offer no proper analogue.
'Unbegotten' as a notion belongs to the Father alone.
